stages.name: Opportunity cost and economic agents
stages.title: Opportunity cost and economic agents
stages.sub: Who faces opportunity cost, and why it matters to each of them.

steps.q: Scarcity means not everyone can have everything. So what must people, firms and governments do?
steps.wrong: Wait until there is enough for everyone
steps.hint: If everything cannot be had at once, what is left to do?

steps.q: When you choose one option, do you still get the ones you did not choose?
steps.hint: You chose the phone. Can you also spend that same money on the holiday?

steps.q: Can the same land, workers and machines be used to make something else instead?
steps.hint: Could a factory make juice or fizzy drinks with the very same resources?

steps.q: Of everything you gave up, which one do you count when judging a choice?
steps.right: The best one you gave up
steps.hint: You can only have one thing instead. Which of the things you gave up would you actually have picked?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: So what is the real cost of a choice?
steps.right: The value of the next best alternative you gave up
steps.wrong: The money you pay, plus the time it takes
steps.hint: Money is only one way of counting. What did you actually give up?

steps.q: A shopper budgets, a bakery picks bread or cakes, a government picks hospitals or roads. Do all three face the same problem?
steps.right: Yes, all are choosing between limited options
steps.wrong: No, only the government's choice counts as economic
steps.hint: Think about whether spending money, using ovens and using tax revenue are really different kinds of problem.

steps.q: A government builds a hospital instead of a road. If it ignores what the road would have given, might it decide badly?
steps.right: Yes, it might choose badly without weighing this up
steps.wrong: No, only the money spent matters
steps.hint: The hospital's true cost is the next best alternative given up. What happens if that is ignored?
